extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy analysts, and students studying Quebec language policy and sociolinguistics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying quantitative indicators used to evaluate language use, integration, and policy effects in Quebec (e.g., language of work, public language indices, income gaps), with attention to controls, sampling and classifications (immigrant origin, age at arrival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of work (usage at workplace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of the language(s) workers use at work, based on census questions about the language used most often at work and languages used regularly; categories include 'uniquement le français' and 'surtout le français'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a component of 'language spoken in public'; distinguishes predominant use from regular use. Important for assessing whether the right to work in French is realized and for measuring contribution to French-language institutions. Data come from census questions (2001, 2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational distribution by mother tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage distribution of francophones, anglophones and allophones across occupational categories (administrators, professionals, technicians) from census data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess group position on the labour market and to detect under- or over-representation; must be interpreted while controlling for schooling and field of study, which strongly determine access to professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for scolarization/education in occupational comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling occupational comparisons for diplomas obtained and field of study because these are primary determinants of access to professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without controlling for education and other determinants, raw occupational percentages are 'peu informatives' and cannot support strong conclusions about discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income gap measure (controlling for non-linguistic factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of earnings between linguistic groups (e.g., francophones vs anglophones), with controls for years of experience, schooling, weeks worked and marital status to isolate language-based discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an index of discrimination — 'toutes choses étant égales par ailleurs'. Example: in 1970 francophone unilingual men earned 20% less than anglophone unilingual men after controls; by 2000 gaps may be statistically insignificant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilingualism vs unilingualism categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of workers as unilingual (one language) or bilingual (claiming regular use of both) to compare outcomes (income, workplace language use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables estimating the 'rentabilité de la connaissance des langues' (profitability of language knowledge); e.g., bilingual francophones' earnings relative to anglophones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Census question combination rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two census questions (language used most often at work; languages used regularly at work) to create categories: 'uniquement le français' and 'surtout le français' (uses French most often but also regularly uses English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination yields distinct groups for analysis of predominant vs secondary language use at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigrant origin classification (influence latine vs other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grouping allophone immigrants into 'd’influence latine' (Latin-language mother tongue or born in a francophone country) versus 'influence autre' (other origins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification is a central determinant in analyses: immigrants of Latin influence show markedly higher French use; conclusions about policy impact hinge on these origin groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age at arrival
rubrics_metrics.description: Splitting immigrants by age at migration (e.g., arrived at 12 or younger vs arrived at 13 or older) to evaluate effects of schooling in Quebec on later language use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Younger arrivals likely attended Quebec secondary schools and show higher French usage at work; used to assess scolarization effect independent of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection / composition adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for changes in the origin composition of immigration over time (selection) when interpreting trends in aggregate language-use percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate decreases in French use among immigrants can be due to shifts in origin composition rather than deterioration of integration; apply simulations or standardization to estimate what would be observed if composition were constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation / adjusted totals for stable immigration origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical simulation estimating language use (e.g., French at work) under the counterfactual that immigration origin composition remained constant over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show whether observed aggregate trends stem from composition changes or from changes within origin groups; figure 14 shows adjusted totals roughly stable (~45%) from 1970–2001.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific public language use indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Indices constructed by grouping survey items about language used in related activities/domains (immediate network, institutional domain, media consumption, work) and an overall general index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistique Canada computed these indices (2006) to summarize language use across domains; annex lists activities for each domain; indices allow domain-by-domain comparison between origin/status groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: General public language-use index
rubrics_metrics.description: An overall index summarizing language used in public/community activities to indicate general orientation of allophones (e.g., % who use mostly French in public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a broader, more predictive indicator of language orientation than home language; used to compare natifs vs immigrants and origin groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The language most often used by francophone native speakers when communicating with anglophone superiors, colleagues and subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important because the right to work in French requires that French be the convergence language in internal communications; internal communications (supervisors/colleagues/subordinates) carry more weight than external communications with clients/suppliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external communications weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Differential importance assigned to types of workplace communication: internal (with supervisors/colleagues/subordinates) considered more decisive for whether French is the normal workplace language than external communications (clients, suppliers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data on internal communications (survey of firms with 100+ employees) inform assessments of whether French is the dominant interlinguistic language at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain exceptions (media consumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that media consumption behaves differently: French usage is less common in media than in other public activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting domain indices, note that media is an exception to overall trends and should be treated accordingly in conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey sample size and disaggregation limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that limited sample sizes (e.g., ~2000 in the 2006 StatCan survey) prevent fine-grained disaggregation, such as isolating immigrants who arrived before 1970.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample limitations constrain which subgroup analyses are feasible and must be reported when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent classification rules for multiple/third languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for categorizing respondents who declared a third language alone or with another: those declaring a third language only are excluded; those declaring a third language plus a public language are counted with the public language users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification choices can shift percentages by a few points; be explicit about grouping method (see note referencing Paul BELAND).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of markers (bold percentages, proximity/distant points) to indicate statistically significant differences between totals by origin, and between natives and various immigrant cohorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results report which differences are statistically significant (e.g., boldface), and significance tests were performed only for the first (general) column; report significance conventions when presenting tables/figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring 'profitability' of language knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating economic returns to knowing French or English by comparing controlled income differences between bilinguals and unilinguals of different mother tongues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess whether knowledge of French benefits anglophones and whether knowledge of English benefits francophones; example: in 1970 French knowledge did not add income for anglophones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs private (home) language distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating language spoken in public as a distinct indicator from mother tongue or language spoken at home; public language is the development of linguistic capital and more predictive of societal language orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy interventions target public domain language use; home language measures reflect accumulated capital and selection effects and are less directly predictive of institutional language dynamics.
